title: Shishak's Invasion and Rehoboam's Humbling
summary: Once his kingdom is secure, Rehoboam and the people abandon the LORD's law, and in his fifth year Shishak of Egypt invades, takes Judah's fortified cities, and reaches Jerusalem. When the prophet Shemaiah declares that God has handed them over, the king and leaders humble themselves, and God spares the city from destruction but lets Shishak strip the temple and palace treasuries. Rehoboam's reign is summed up as evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.
story: Chapter 11 ended with three good years in which Judah walked in the way of David and Solomon. This chapter tells what came next, and it sets the pattern the Chronicler will use for every king that follows: faithfulness brings strength, strength tempts a king to forget God, unfaithfulness brings trouble, and humbling oneself before God brings mercy. Solomon's golden age ends here in a very visible way, as the gold shields made for the palace (1 Kings 10:16-17; 2 Chronicles 9:15-16) are carried off to Egypt and replaced with bronze. Rehoboam dies, and his son Abijah takes the throne in chapter 13.
historical:
Shishak is the Egyptian pharaoh known from Egyptian sources as Sheshonq I, founder of Egypt's Twenty-second Dynasty, a line of rulers of Libyan descent. His invasion is one of the earliest events in the history of the kings of Israel and Judah that can be connected with an outside record. On a wall of the great temple of Amun at Karnak (at Thebes, modern Luxor), Sheshonq left a triumphal relief listing many towns in the land of Canaan that he claimed to have subdued, and a fragment of a stela bearing his name was found at Megiddo in northern Israel. The campaign is usually dated to about 925 BC. Jerusalem does not appear among the names that survive on the Karnak list, which is damaged in places, and scholars read that silence in different ways. Many think the biblical account of Rehoboam paying off Shishak with the temple and palace treasures explains why the city itself was not besieged or destroyed.

The parallel in 1 Kings 14:25-28 records the invasion and the loss of the gold shields. Chronicles adds the size of the army, the capture of the fortified cities, Shemaiah's prophecy, and the king's repentance, which give the event its theological meaning for the Chronicler's readers, who knew what it was to be subject to foreign kings.
cultural:
The Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites of verse 3 were peoples who served in Egyptian armies. Libya lay to Egypt's west, Cush (sometimes rendered Ethiopia) lay to the south along the upper Nile in what is now Sudan, and the Sukkites are otherwise unknown, though they are usually thought to be a group from the Libyan desert or the regions near Egypt. A king's gold ceremonial shields were symbols of wealth and prestige carried in royal processions. Replacing them with bronze kept up the ceremony while exposing how much had been lost, and the detail that the guards carefully returned the bronze shields to the guardroom after each use adds a touch of irony.

Verse 13 names Rehoboam's mother, Naamah, an Ammonite. The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan, and Solomon had married foreign women from among them (1 Kings 11:1). The formal notice of the queen mother is standard in the books of Kings and Chronicles, and the Chronicler's readers would have noticed that Solomon's heir was half Ammonite.
literary: This chapter is a compact example of what scholars call the Chronicler's theology of immediate retribution: the results of faithfulness or unfaithfulness show up within a king's own reign rather than generations later. The sequence is plain: established, forsook, invaded, warned, humbled, spared. The verb humble occurs four times (verses 6, 7 twice, and 12), which makes it the chapter's hinge. Shemaiah's word contains a play on the verb forsake: "You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak." The closing formula in verses 13 to 16 follows the pattern Chronicles uses for every king (age, length of reign, mother, verdict, sources, burial), and verse 14 gives the verdict that explains the whole reign: he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.

outline.t: Rehoboam forsakes the law, and Shishak invades
Shemaiah's warning and the leaders' humbling
The treasures taken, bronze shields for gold, and a partial reprieve
Summary of Rehoboam's reign and his death

doctrines.note: The king and leaders humble themselves and confess that the LORD is righteous, and God turns his anger away. Chronicles repeatedly shows that humbling oneself before God is never wasted, even when consequences remain.

God's judgment is measured and purposeful. He does not destroy Jerusalem, but he lets Judah serve Shishak so that they may learn the difference between serving God and serving foreign kings. Discipline here aims at teaching, not only at punishment.
The chapter shows how sin often follows success. Once Rehoboam's power was established, he forsook the law, and the root is named in verse 14: a heart that never set itself to seek the LORD.

words.note: Kana, to humble oneself, to be brought low. This is a key word in Chronicles and a central part of God's promise in 2 Chronicles 7:14. It describes a deliberate lowering of oneself before God, admitting fault and dependence. Here it appears four times and turns the chapter from destruction to reprieve.

Ma'al, to act unfaithfully. The word describes a breach of trust, especially taking or misusing what belongs to God. It is one of the Chronicler's main words for the sin that finally led to the exile (1 Chronicles 9:1). Its use in verse 2 frames Shishak's invasion as a consequence of betrayal, not an accident of politics.

Azav, to leave or forsake. The chapter uses it for Judah abandoning the law and for God abandoning them to Shishak. The mirror between the two uses expresses a principle stated earlier by the prophet Azariah in chapter 15:2 and by God in 1 Chronicles 28:9: those who forsake the LORD will be forsaken.

Avodah, service or labor. The word covers both the worship of God and forced work for a human master. Verse 8 plays on that range: Judah will serve Shishak so that they learn the difference between serving God and serving the kings of other lands.

christ: Verse 8 names the choice the whole Bible puts before God's people: whose service will they accept? Judah learned by painful comparison that serving the LORD was lighter than serving Egypt. Jesus made the same contrast when he invited the weary to take his yoke, which he said was easy and light (Matthew 11:28-30), and Paul describes Christians as freed from one kind of slavery into a willing service to God (Romans 6:17-22). The chapter's pattern of humbling and mercy also anticipates the gospel's promise that God gives grace to the humble (James 4:6, 1 Peter 5:5-6), and it finds its deepest form in Christ, who humbled himself to the point of death and was exalted (Philippians 2:8-9). These are thematic links, not predictions in the text.

hard.q: Does the Chronicler teach that every disaster is punishment for a specific sin?
hard.a: Chronicles often links a king's faithfulness to blessing and his unfaithfulness to trouble within his own reign, and this chapter is a clear case. Some readers take this as a general rule for how God governs history. Most interpreters, however, note that the Chronicler is writing theological history about the covenant king and people of Judah, where the prophets explicitly interpret events, as Shemaiah does here. Other parts of Scripture, including Job, many psalms, and Jesus' words about the tower of Siloam and the man born blind (Luke 13:1-5, John 9:1-3), warn against reading every suffering as a direct penalty. The Chronicler's pattern is best read as a call to his readers to seek God and humble themselves, not as a formula for diagnosing other people's troubles.

questions: Rehoboam forsook God's law after he became strong. Why do seasons of security often become seasons of spiritual drift?
Judah's leaders said “The LORD is righteous” when they were under judgment. What does it look like to humble yourself without excuses?
Bronze shields replaced gold ones, and the ceremony went on. Where might you be keeping up appearances after something real has been lost?
